title: The Gang Recycles Their Trash

jokes.text: I can't believe the trashmen can strike in this economy. It's unbelievable. It should be against the law.
jokes.setup: The gang is complaining about trash piling up outside the bar
jokes.punchline: Frank's knee-jerk anti-worker sentiment delivered as moral outrage — the punchline is how confidently wrong he is
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank — entitled, out-of-touch, delivered with full conviction. Works because it's character-specific but isn't a memorable line on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Shut up, bird.

jokes.text: Is all of this our trash? We generate a ton of it. It's a sad throwaway culture we're living in.
jokes.setup: They're surrounded by their own overflowing garbage
jokes.punchline: One of them solemnly laments 'throwaway culture' while standing in a mountain of trash they themselves created — total lack of self-awareness
jokes.explanation: The irony is well-constructed — the gang has zero self-awareness and the juxtaposition of their trash mountain with their philosophical musing is a clean joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: These guys are blasting us in the ass.

jokes.text: I feel like you guys have done something like that before? Have we? Shut up, bird.
jokes.setup: Dee notices the situation feels familiar — a callback to previous episodes of the gang doing the same thing
jokes.punchline: The gang dismisses her meta-awareness with 'Shut up, bird' — the first instance of the episode's central running gag where they refuse to acknowledge the repetition
jokes.explanation: This is the seed of the episode's central conceit — meta-awareness about the show recycling its own plots. 'Shut up, bird' is a great dismissal and Dee's role as the ignored voice of reason is perfect character work. High rewatch value because on rewatch you know exactly where this is going.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Who am I supposed to vote for, the Republican who's blasting me in the ass or the Democrat who's blasting me in the ass?

jokes.text: These guys are blasting us in the ass... we pay their salaries, and they turn around and ass-blast us.
jokes.setup: Frank complaining about the striking trashmen
jokes.punchline: The repeated use of 'ass-blast' as a political metaphor delivered with total sincerity — the phrasing is so crude it becomes absurd
jokes.explanation: Frank's rhetorical vocabulary reducing political economics to anal violation is very on-brand. The repetition of 'ass-blast' escalates it from a slip of the tongue to a chosen worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, politics is all one big ass-blast.

jokes.text: Who am I supposed to vote for, the Republican who's blasting me in the ass or the Democrat who's blasting me in the ass? Yeah, politics is all one big ass-blast.
jokes.setup: Someone points out Frank doesn't pay taxes or vote
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'both sides' political philosophy expressed entirely through the ass-blast metaphor — a surprisingly coherent if vulgar political statement
jokes.explanation: The escalation from general complaint to fully-formed political philosophy stated in ass-blast terms is funny and surprisingly sharp. The joke works on two levels: Frank's crudeness and the accidental political satire of both-sides-ism.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Let's pull up our bootstraps, oil up a couple asses and do a little plowing of our own. Pow!

jokes.text: Let's pull up our bootstraps, oil up a couple asses and do a little plowing of our own.
jokes.setup: Frank rallying the gang to take over the trash business
jokes.punchline: The 'pull up your bootstraps' idiom is immediately corrupted into an extended sexual metaphor about oiling asses — the inspirational speech becomes pornographic
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed bit where the motivational language slides seamlessly into unintentional sexual innuendo. The commitment to the metaphor ('oil up a couple asses') makes it funnier than a simple crude statement.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Not gay sex.

jokes.text: Not gay sex. Okay, yeah. It seemed like... What are you talking about? We're gonna solve the trash crisis.
jokes.setup: Frank's 'oiling asses and plowing' speech ends with a 'Pow!'
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately clarifies 'Not gay sex' — which only makes it worse, and the gang scrambles to move past it
jokes.explanation: Mac's clarification is funnier than the original innuendo because it reveals he was thinking about it. Given Mac's closeted gay arc throughout the series, this lands especially hard on rewatch. The quick pivot to 'We're gonna solve the trash crisis' is a great awkward recovery.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Okay, yeah. It seemed like... What are you talking about?

jokes.text: All of this, I've heard all of this before. No? Shut up, bird.
jokes.setup: Dee again tries to point out they've done all this before
jokes.punchline: Second 'Shut up, bird' — the running gag is established; the gang doubles down on ignoring the meta-commentary
jokes.explanation: The second repetition confirms the running gag and deepens the meta-joke. Dee's growing frustration at being dismissed while being completely correct is core to her character. Good economy — two words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Shut up, bird.

jokes.text: Meanwhile, I dress Dee up like a whore, get a city official, bribe him, and make him give us the contract, undermining the trash unions.
jokes.setup: Frank presenting his elaborate trash crisis plan
jokes.punchline: The plan casually includes 'I dress Dee up like a whore' as a standard operational step — delivered with the same matter-of-fact tone as renting the van
jokes.explanation: Frank's breezy inclusion of 'dress Dee as a whore' in his logistics plan — sandwiched between mundane details — is classic Always Sunny. The normalcy of his delivery is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Meanwhile, I dress Dee up like a whore, get a city official, bribe him, and make him give us the contract

jokes.text: We've gone to door-to-door in a van before, and that didn't work out for us.
jokes.setup: Frank presenting the door-to-door van plan as new
jokes.punchline: Charlie acknowledges they've done this exact thing before — another instance of the gang being aware but still proceeding
jokes.explanation: Continues the meta-awareness thread but is less punchy than the 'Shut up, bird' versions. Works more as texture for the running gag than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We've gone to door-to-door in a van before, and that didn't work out for us.

jokes.text: I don't want to be a trashman. I'll bribe the city official with you. I need a lady whore. Dee? Yeah, I've done the whore thing before. I don't care for it. I won't be doing it again.
jokes.setup: Frank assigns roles; Dee is assigned to be the whore again
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat 'I don't care for it. I won't be doing it again.' — delivered as if she's declining a job she's quit, then immediately capitulates
jokes.explanation: Dee's resignation — 'I don't care for it' as if reviewing a restaurant — is excellent character work. The implied capitulation makes it sadder and funnier simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: How often should it work out?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Almost never.

jokes.text: How many times have we done this kind of thing before? Almost never. That's because you don't listen to me. This time we do it my way.
jokes.setup: Dee pressing the gang on how often their plans work
jokes.punchline: 'Almost never' — the gang admits their plans almost never work but charge ahead anyway, with Frank insisting this time it's different
jokes.explanation: The 'almost never' admission is funny for its honesty and the immediate pivot to 'this time it's different' captures a universal human delusion. Good structural beat that deepens the episode's thesis.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: And I'm still the wild card, so that's good.

jokes.text: So, Frank is the brains and you're just the looks now? And I'm still the wild card, so that's good.
jokes.setup: Mac questioning the new group dynamic where Frank leads
jokes.punchline: Charlie cheerfully confirming he's still the wild card — taking genuine pride in being the most chaotic and useless member
jokes.explanation: Charlie's pride in being the wild card — as though it's a prestigious title — is a perfect Charlie moment. The 'so that's good' is the ideal understated button. High character integration score because only Charlie could deliver this with this level of genuine satisfaction.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I feel like you just agreed with me, but you weren't listening to what I was saying.

jokes.text: Nobody wants a wild card, okay? It doesn't make any sense. We don't want a maniac in our group. There's no benefit to it.
jokes.setup: Dennis trying to reform the group dynamic
jokes.punchline: Dennis, one of the most destructive and narcissistic people in the group, earnestly arguing there's 'no benefit' to a maniac — with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: The irony of Dennis — a deeply unhinged person — being the voice against chaos is funny but underplayed here. Works better as character texture than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I feel like you just agreed with me, but you weren't listening to what I was saying.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You pointed at me like I said something, but I didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Good.

jokes.text: Charlie, having somebody making wild decisions that make no sense, that benefits nobody. Yes. Right, yes. Is he listening to us? I can't tell. He's listening. He's not understanding.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac explaining to Charlie why the wild card role is bad
jokes.punchline: Charlie affirms enthusiastically but clearly hasn't understood a word — his affirmations are disconnected from the actual content, which Mac and Dennis then narrate
jokes.explanation: The layered joke of Charlie's enthusiastic agreement with something he fundamentally doesn't understand, followed by Mac and Dennis narrating the disconnect in real time, is a sharp piece of character comedy. 'He's listening. He's not understanding' is a great two-line beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, he doesn't even like, get us, man. It's... We're talking about you.

jokes.text: What do you think is happening right now?
jokes.setup: Mac asks Charlie what he thinks is going on as they discuss him
jokes.punchline: The question is directed at Charlie who has been obliviously affirming everything — the reveal of how little he's tracked is left implicit
jokes.explanation: A beat that extends joke #15 but doesn't add much. Functions as a grace note rather than its own joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure, in the 1950s, yeah, you could drive around door to door in a windowless van, and people didn't think they were gonna get raped. Now, th-they will think that.

jokes.text: In the 1950s, yeah, you could drive around door to door in a windowless van, and people didn't think they were gonna get raped. Now, they will think that.
jokes.setup: The gang arguing that Frank's plan is 'outdated'
jokes.punchline: Dennis's specific concern about the windowless van is not that it looks unprofessional, but that it now reads as a rape vehicle — framed as a simple logistical update
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The historical framing ('in the 1950s') gives it false authority, the dark specificity of 'get raped' as the concern (not 'look suspicious') is characteristically Dennis, and the matter-of-fact delivery makes it land hard. High quotability, strong structure, economical. Dennis's awareness of rape optics while remaining oblivious to his own predatory tendencies is rich irony.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You're presenting yourself as a banana.

jokes.text: With the tuxedos, you know, honestly, who wouldn't want their trashman in a tuxedo? Absolutely. I know I would.
jokes.setup: The gang 'improving' Frank's plan by upgrading the van to a limo and wearing tuxedos
jokes.punchline: Dennis sincerely arguing the tuxedo upgrade is consumer-friendly — the absurdity of tuxedo trashmen presented as obvious market wisdom
jokes.explanation: Funny primarily because of the absurdist confidence — 'who wouldn't want their trashman in a tuxedo' said like it's self-evident. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I did not picture this guy getting recycled back into the mix.

jokes.text: Wonder how Mac is doing back there. [cut to Mac hanging off back of moving limo covered in trash, clearly miserable]
jokes.setup: Mac earlier expressed he couldn't hang off the back of a vehicle like a real trashman
jokes.punchline: Mac is nonetheless hanging off the back of the limo, covered in trash — the callback to his stated impossibility now rendered as miserable reality
jokes.explanation: A satisfying visual callback — the economy of 'Wonder how Mac is doing back there' followed by the implied cut to suffering Mac is classic sitcom structure executed well. The visual does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: ♪ I still got the moves... ♪

jokes.text: You're supposed to look like a whore. The whore-politician is outdated, Frank. That is an idea that's best left in the trash.
jokes.setup: Frank wants Dee to dress as a whore to seduce the city official
jokes.punchline: Dee refusing and calling the 'whore-politician' scheme outdated — delivered with surprising dignity — while also inadvertently making a trash-themed pun ('best left in the trash')
jokes.explanation: Dee's principled stand — calling it 'outdated' rather than wrong — is a funny distinction. The accidental trash pun is a nice bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: ♪ I still got the moves... ♪

jokes.text: You're presenting yourself as a banana.
jokes.setup: Dee insists she's presenting herself as a 'powerful lady' rather than a whore
jokes.punchline: Frank's flat assessment that her outfit looks like a banana — which is both a devastating put-down and an absurd visual detail
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Maximum economy — four words do enormous work. The specificity of 'banana' (not just 'yellow' or 'ridiculous') is perfect absurdist comedy. Frank's flat delivery makes it devastating. The visual of Dee in a banana-yellow power suit sells it completely. Genuinely quotable, highly original in its specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Let's not do accents. That's the kind of wild-card stuff that always gets us into trouble.

jokes.text: Frank physically grabbing Dee's outfit and ripping it open to 'sex it up' — Dee screaming 'Get off me!' 'Stop it, Frank!' as he fondles her clothing
jokes.setup: Frank wants Dee to show more skin; Dee refuses
jokes.punchline: Frank doesn't argue further — he just physically starts pulling at her clothes while she screams, treating it as a wardrobe problem he's solving
jokes.explanation: Frank's total dismissal of consent framed as pragmatism is characteristically dark Always Sunny. The visual of an old man manhandling a woman's blazer while she screams is cringe comedy that works because of its commitment. 'Now it looks good' after he ruins it is the button.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mac, you have an exceptional number of bugs in your teeth.

jokes.text: Get off me! / Show some skin. / Stop it, Frank! / Great! / This is nice. This doesn't look powerful or sexy. / Now it looks good. / Great job, Frank!
jokes.setup: Frank wants Dee to open her buttons to 'sex it up'; Dee refuses; Frank apparently physically grabs at her clothes
jokes.punchline: Frank apparently succeeds in undoing her outfit against her will, then compliments himself — 'Great job, Frank!' — while Dee screams; the sarcastic 'Now it looks good' implies the result is chaotic and undignified
jokes.explanation: Physical cringe comedy inferred from dialogue — Frank's self-congratulation while physically accosting Dee is very on-brand. The 'Great job, Frank!' from Frank to himself is the best beat. Loses points for being somewhat predictable Frank-Dee abuse.

dialogue.line: ♪ Hello, We bet you hate that smell, That smell from all your trash ♪

jokes.text: It's the gay guy who wanted to buy Paddy's. Yeah, you fired me from the Oldies Rock Café. I did not picture this guy getting recycled back into the mix.
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee arrive to bribe the city official and discover it's a character they've encountered before
jokes.punchline: Frank's fourth-wall-grazing assessment: 'I did not picture this guy getting recycled back into the mix' — an in-universe line that doubles as a writer's room joke about recycling characters
jokes.explanation: The word 'recycled' in the context of an episode literally about recycling plots is a sharp meta-joke. Frank doesn't realize he's making a meta-comment, which makes it funnier. Strong earned-vs-cheap score because it works on multiple levels simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Wait, I have to stop you. Damn it, Dennis. I knew this wasn't gonna work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, the plan was good.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie, you were sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I was...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You were a little sharp.

jokes.text: So much for the sex appeal angle. I don't know, Frank, why don't you sex it up a little? ...How about you be the whore?
jokes.setup: Their plan to use sex appeal on the city official has failed because it's the gay guy they already know
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately turns Frank's own logic on him — 'How about you be the whore?' — and then proceeds to physically grab at him in exact mirror of what he did to her
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback — Dee reverses the earlier scene beat-for-beat on Frank. 'How about you be the whore?' lands hard, and Frank's screaming mirror of Dee's earlier protests ('Get off of me!') is a satisfying structural payoff. The city official's 'He likes it like that' button is excellent. High character integration — only this dynamic could produce this reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The elaborate door-to-door sales song about trash collection

jokes.text: ♪ I still got the moves... ♪ [Frank apparently dancing/posing provocatively for the city official]
jokes.setup: Dee and Frank arguing about who should be the whore
jokes.punchline: Frank apparently breaks into a seductive song/dance — the horror of old, gross Frank performing sensually is the entire joke
jokes.explanation: DeVito doing a seductive dance as Frank would be visually hilarious. The song fragment '♪ I still got the moves' is funnier as a snippet than it would be as a full performance.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: My hunch is that this gentleman has gone from a twink to a twunk to a twank.

jokes.text: Now, right off the bat, Charlie, were you planning on doing an accent of any kind? Yes. Me, too. You guys were both planning on doing accents. Yeah. Of course. Let's not do accents. That's the kind of wild-card stuff that always gets us into trouble.
jokes.setup: Dennis trying to run a disciplined door-to-door approach
jokes.punchline: Both Charlie AND Mac were independently planning to do accents for no reason — 'Of course' said as though it's obvious — revealing the gang's default chaos level
jokes.explanation: The reveal that both Mac AND Charlie had accents planned is funnier than if it were just one of them. 'Of course' as Mac's response to being caught is excellent character work — to him, an unprompted accent is baseline professionalism. Dennis's weary management of these men is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What's a twunk?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Twink and a hunk. A twink with muscles, but still hairless. So smooth. Incredibly smooth.

jokes.text: I have a knife. Why do you have a knife? To make sure that the plan works.
jokes.setup: Dennis asking everyone to put their cards on the table before the pitch
jokes.punchline: Charlie produced a knife, with the completely logical-to-him explanation that it ensures the plan works
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'To make sure that the plan works' is an absolutely perfect Charlie answer — it's not aggressive, not random, just deeply weird logic that Charlie finds self-evident. The knife's causal relationship to plan success is never explained because Charlie sees no need to explain it. Pure character comedy with razor-sharp economy. Highly quotable, strong structure. Comparable to the calibration anchors in terms of character-specific brilliance.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Twank is no good. That's a twink and a skank. Essentially a ragdoll, just being passed around from twink to twunk to bear to otter.

jokes.text: I'm afraid that if I don't have the knife, then one of you will stab somebody. And again, that's a wild card thing; we don't want that.
jokes.setup: Everyone debating who should hold Charlie's knife
jokes.punchline: Dennis's reasoning for taking the knife is that he's afraid someone else will stab a person — not that the knife shouldn't exist, but that he should control it. His responsible framing only highlights the insanity.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's self-appointed knife stewardship is funny because his concern is not 'why is there a knife' but 'who has the knife.' It naturalizes the absurdity of the knife existing, which is very Always Sunny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: the otter generates his power through extraordinary quickness, cunning, and skill.

jokes.text: Mac, you have an exceptional number of bugs in your teeth. You're gonna want to rinse those out; it's disgusting.
jokes.setup: Mac was apparently riding in an open vehicle
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers 'exceptional number of bugs in your teeth' with clinical precision — 'exceptional NUMBER' as though running an audit of Mac's dental insect population
jokes.explanation: The word 'exceptional' doing enormous work here — it implies Dennis has seen normal bug counts and this exceeds that. Dennis's delivery of gross physical observations with bureaucratic precision is very character-specific. 'Exceptional number of bugs' is a memorably specific phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Some cocks can't be unsucked.

jokes.text: ♪ Hello / We bet you hate that smell / That smell / That smell from all your trash / Your trash / We bet you'd like three charming men to take your trash from you / From you / We have a limousine / A limousine / That we can fill fill with trash...♪
jokes.setup: Three grown men in tuxedos at a stranger's door
jokes.punchline: The song's lyrics are sincere, slightly repetitive, and oddly echo-structured — 'fill fill with trash' — the earnestness of the performance sells the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The song's earnest awfulness is calibrated perfectly — it's not trying to be a parody of a jingle; it IS a jingle, written by Charlie, which is worse. The 'fill fill' repetition is a great accidental stumble. Part of a larger comedic sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I, for one, am of the belief that some things can't be thrown in the trash, Frank. And your sexuality is one of them.

jokes.text: Damn it, Dennis. I knew this wasn't gonna work. No, the plan was good. Charlie, you were sharp. I was... You were a little sharp.
jokes.setup: The homeowner interrupts the song mid-performance
jokes.punchline: Everyone immediately assumes the song failed — before realizing the homeowner is HIRING them. The gang arguing about whether Charlie was 'a little sharp' reveals they're more worried about musical quality than business results.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is well-executed — interruption reads as failure, then revealed as success. The 'little sharp' debate adds a layer of absurdity. Good structural beat.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I forgot.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, I guess we'll be the ones to slink away.

jokes.text: Did you say you would take my trash? Yeah. Yeah, that's... My... How much will it cost? $200... That's fantastic. Can we start now? Yeah! One more time with the song? No thank you. Just the trash.
jokes.setup: Gang feared the song failed; the homeowner is enthusiastically hiring them
jokes.punchline: 'One more time with the song? No thank you. Just the trash.' — the homeowner politely but firmly declining an encore while still being a customer is a perfect button
jokes.explanation: 'No thank you. Just the trash.' is a great line — polite, complete, perfectly timed. The homeowner as a straight-man character who accepts the absurd premise but draws a clear line at a second performance is a good comedic device.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: The gulls are shitting all over me.

jokes.text: So how does this place tickle your fancy? Because you are a power bottom.
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee have taken the city official to a venue to try to bribe/seduce him
jokes.punchline: Dee asking why they're at this particular venue; Frank explaining it's because the official 'is a power bottom' — said as analysis, not insult
jokes.explanation: Frank deploying 'power bottom' as a clinical assessment of the official's gay identity — and therefore his bribery leverage — is characteristically unhinged. His matter-of-fact gay subculture knowledge is a recurring Frank joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Let's just dump it in a poor neighborhood because they don't mind living in their own filth.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Absolutely. They don't know any better.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I mean, why else would they choose to live like that?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: They don't care?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: They clearly don't care.

jokes.text: We take you to a titty bar and you say no to us. We bring you to this place with all these juicy dongs, and you shut us down. What team are you playing for?
jokes.setup: The city official refuses to be bribed or seduced at either venue
jokes.punchline: Frank's confused summary of events — moving from 'titty bar' to 'juicy dongs' and still getting nothing — framed as a logic problem Frank cannot solve
jokes.explanation: 'Juicy dongs' as Frank's sincere description of the venue is a good Frank-ism. The binary logic — titty bar OR dongs — as his complete map of human sexuality is very character-specific. 'What team are you playing for?' as the exasperated conclusion is a solid button.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: let's just dump it in a poor neighborhood because they don't mind living in their own filth.

jokes.text: I think I know what's going on here. This man has been realigned. He's a yestergay.
jokes.setup: Frank can't figure out why the official responds to neither women nor men
jokes.punchline: Dee confidently introduces the term 'yestergay' — a person who used to be gay — as though it's established clinical vocabulary
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best original coinages. 'Yestergay' is a brilliantly economical portmanteau — 'yesterday' + 'gay' — capturing the idea of a formerly-gay person who has 'converted.' The confidence with which Dee deploys it, as though it's an established term she's read about, is perfect. High originality, excellent economy, strong earned-vs-cheap because the word earns its laugh through genuine wit rather than shock value alone. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: He just tried to kiss me.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, he did a little bit.

jokes.text: A lot of men bounce around from label to label never quite finding their proper gay home. My hunch is that this gentleman has gone from a twink to a twunk to a twank.
jokes.setup: Dee elaborating on the 'yestergay' concept
jokes.punchline: The taxonomic journey from 'twink to twunk to twank' — each slightly worse than the last — delivered as confident academic analysis
jokes.explanation: The escalating portmanteau sequence — twink/twunk/twank — is brilliantly constructed comedy writing. Each term is a real or plausible blend, and the sequence has a natural narrative arc (twunk is aspirational; twank is a warning). Dee's confident academic register makes it funnier. The writing here is genuinely impressive and distinctive.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He's trying to confuse us with his fancy language and his expensive podiums

jokes.text: What's a twunk? Twink and a hunk. A twink with muscles, but still hairless. So smooth. Incredibly smooth.
jokes.setup: Frank asking for clarification on the twunk definition
jokes.punchline: The definition escalates into Mac adding 'So smooth. Incredibly smooth' — unprompted, with apparent longing — revealing Mac's inner monologue about hairless men
jokes.explanation: Mac's unprompted elaboration on smoothness — 'So smooth. Incredibly smooth' — is a character comedy goldmine. This is Mac's closeted gay arc surfacing in real time, and the two short sentences do enormous work. High character integration because only Mac's specific situation makes this funny. 'Incredibly smooth' as a second sentence is the right amount of commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Hey, y'all, it's me, Martina Martinez.

jokes.text: A twank on the other hand. Twank is no good. That's a twink and a skank. Essentially a ragdoll, just being passed around from twink to twunk to bear to otter.
jokes.setup: Continuing the gay subculture taxonomy
jokes.punchline: 'Essentially a ragdoll, just being passed around' — the twank definition escalates from portmanteau to dark character sketch
jokes.explanation: 'Essentially a ragdoll, just being passed around from twink to twunk to bear to otter' is a vivid, specific, dark image. The escalation from classification to narrative is well-constructed. 'Ragdoll' is a great word choice.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Rape! Rape! Rape! My... This white boy's got his hands all over my beautiful brown body!

jokes.text: What's an otter? Subsection of bear. Still hairy, but where a bear generates his power through sheer mass alone, the otter generates his power through extraordinary quickness, cunning, and skill.
jokes.setup: Frank asking about the 'otter' in the taxonomy
jokes.punchline: Mac delivers a detailed, respectful, almost admiring breakdown of the otter's power — treating it like a nature documentary about gay subculture
jokes.explanation: Mac taking over from Dee to deliver an authoritative otter briefing — 'extraordinary quickness, cunning, and skill' — is both a great standalone absurdist joke and a perfect Mac character moment. His encyclopedic knowledge and clear respect for the otter's attributes ('generates his power') is delightful and deeply character-specific. The nature-documentary register is inspired.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: When was the last time a white lady pick up after you when you threw your orange soda and your grape sodas on the ground?!

jokes.text: That is a lot to keep in your head to maintain a lifestyle.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee completing the elaborate gay subculture taxonomy
jokes.punchline: Frank's response is not about the subject matter but about the cognitive burden of tracking all of it — said with genuine sympathy
jokes.explanation: Frank's genuine concern about the informational load of maintaining a gay identity is a great button on the taxonomy sequence. It's not homophobic — he seems impressed and sympathetic. The deadpan delivery of a surprisingly empathetic observation is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Look, it would've been fine if Dee hadn't incited a race war.

jokes.text: It's very difficult to maintain the lifestyle of a twank versatile 'cause this often leads to a lot of self-hatred and denial, especially among the religious or political types. So they try and realign their sexual orientation through therapy.
jokes.setup: Continuing the academic analysis of the yestergay phenomenon
jokes.punchline: Dee's clinical summary of the conversion therapy pathway — framed as logical brand management rather than a traumatic experience — lands as dark satire
jokes.explanation: Dee treating conversion therapy as a consumer behavior pattern — 'realign their sexual orientation' said like a brand repositioning — is effective dark comedy. The Always Sunny approach of making horrible things sound mundane works here.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We should make rugs for the bar. That's a good idea.

jokes.text: Some things can't be thrown in the trash, Frank. And your sexuality is one of them. I totally agree. Some cocks can't be unsucked.
jokes.setup: Dee making a philosophical point about sexual identity being immutable
jokes.punchline: Frank's agreement rendered in the most blunt possible terms: 'Some cocks can't be unsucked.' — a filthy but logically consistent restatement of Dee's point
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines and arguably one of the series' most quotable Frank-isms. The structure is perfect: Dee makes an elegant metaphorical statement using the episode's own trash motif ('can't be thrown in the trash'), then Frank translates it into the most literal, anatomical terms possible. The parallel structure ('can't be thrown' / 'can't be unsucked') gives it formal elegance wrapped in pure vulgarity. Maximum economy — five words crystallize the entire yestergay argument. Only Frank delivers this line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He's a twink versatile. You watch yourself. I wouldn't be able to satisfy him.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: A twink versatile? That's impressive.

jokes.text: Still gay. You still here? I thought you'd be gone by now. I can't. You're pointing a gun at me. I forgot.
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee making their philosophical pronouncements about gay identity
jokes.punchline: The city official is still there because Frank has been pointing a gun at him — Frank FORGOT he was holding a gun. The entire elaborate taxonomy was delivered at gunpoint.
jokes.explanation: Structurally brilliant. The entire gay taxonomy sequence — delivered with such earnest academic detail — retroactively becomes a hostage situation. 'I can't. You're pointing a gun at me. I forgot.' is a perfect three-beat reveal. Frank forgetting he was holding a gun is both the punchline and an indictment of everything that just happened. The rewatch value is enormous because every moment in the taxonomy takes on a new dimension. This is excellent Always Sunny writing.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Did you cut the brakes again?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yep.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why would you do that, Charlie?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's just what I do. Wild card, bitches!

jokes.text: Look, yes, we're making lots of money, and that's great, but our tuxes are ruined and our limousine is covered in trash and seagulls. The gulls are shitting all over me.
jokes.setup: The gang is successfully running their trash collection business
jokes.punchline: Dennis's complaint isn't about the hard work — it's about the aesthetic degradation of the tuxedos and limo. The seagulls are an escalating physical indignity.
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the tuxedo conceit — they're now garbage-covered and seagull-bombed — is satisfying. Dennis's concern for the aesthetics rather than the labor is on-brand. 'The gulls are shitting all over me' as Mac's separate complaint adds a good escalation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Try the brakes. Try the... Did you cut the brakes again?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yep.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie. Why would you do that, Charlie?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's just what I do. Wild card, bitches!

jokes.text: Look, we've essentially become garbagemen. That's what I was trying to avoid.
jokes.setup: The gang running a successful but increasingly degrading trash business
jokes.punchline: Dennis stating the obvious with the gravity of a tragedy — the whole point of the plan was to profit from trash collection, but somehow becoming a garbageman was not in the vision
jokes.explanation: Dennis's horror at the logical endpoint of their trash business plan is a good ironic beat. His distinction between 'profiting from trash collection' and 'being a garbageman' makes no practical sense, but makes perfect Dennis sense.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So, the rugs?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, the rugs. It's always been the rugs.

jokes.text: I would like to take one of our old plans out of the trash and recycle it. You want to sell gas door-to-door? I've been thinking it the entire time. That's what I was thinking.
jokes.setup: Charlie suggesting they abandon Frank's plan
jokes.punchline: Charlie's trash/recycle metaphor used to introduce returning to an OLDER plan — which Mac and Dennis had also been thinking about simultaneously — the telepathy of people who always do the same thing
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke crystallizes here — the gang is literally recycling a previous plan, using trash metaphors, in a trash-themed episode. 'I've been thinking it the entire time. That's what I was thinking.' showing that all three had the same nostalgic bad idea simultaneously is a great beat. The episode's thesis made concrete.

jokes.text: Instead of taking that all the way to New Jersey, let's just dump it in a poor neighborhood because they don't mind living in their own filth. Absolutely. They don't know any better. I mean, why else would they choose to live like that? They don't care?
jokes.setup: The gang deciding what to do with the collected trash
jokes.punchline: Mac's casually racist/classist suggestion to dump trash in a poor neighborhood — not as malice but as logistics — with the gang enthusiastically agreeing using the circular logic that poor people must prefer trash
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny darkness — the gang's casual classism and racism isn't presented as villainy but as normal business thinking. 'They don't know any better... why else would they choose to live like that?' is a sharp satire of real-world rationalizations for environmental racism. The confidence of the logic makes it land harder. High character integration — this is exactly the gang's specific flavor of awfulness.

jokes.text: ♪ The boys are back in town... ♪ [the gang triumphantly drives away to dump trash in a poor neighborhood]
jokes.setup: The gang celebrating their decision to illegally dump trash
jokes.punchline: The triumphant 'Boys Are Back in Town' needle drop accompanying what is objectively an awful plan — the music frames their environmental crime as a heroic comeback
jokes.explanation: The ironic triumphant music over an act of illegal dumping is a good use of the needle drop for comedy. The juxtaposition of heroic framing and terrible action is a reliable Always Sunny device.

jokes.text: He just tried to kiss me. Yeah, he did a little bit.
jokes.setup: The triumphant 'Boys Are Back in Town' moment
jokes.punchline: Mac noting matter-of-factly that Charlie just tried to kiss him — Dennis confirming with equal casualness — presented as a minor footnote to the celebration
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'Yeah, he did a little bit' as Mac's reaction to a Charlie kiss attempt is very funny — not outrage, not curiosity, just mild acknowledgment. The minimalism of Mac's confirmation does the work. Good economy.

jokes.text: Brothers, I don't know about you, but I can't understand this college boy's language. Am I right? We gotta have it in plain English.
jokes.setup: Charlie has infiltrated the trashworkers' union meeting disguised as a union agitator
jokes.punchline: Charlie calling the union negotiator's language incomprehensible 'college boy language' — when Charlie himself is barely literate — and presenting himself as the working-class everyman
jokes.explanation: Charlie, who can barely read and writes in bizarre phonetic scrambles, calling someone else's language inaccessible 'college talk' is rich irony. His working-class populist persona is entirely unearned but completely committed. 'Am I right?' as a rhetorical rally works because Charlie has absolutely no idea what he's doing.

jokes.text: He's trying to confuse us with his fancy language and his expensive podiums, but we know the truth. I don't.
jokes.setup: Charlie rallying workers against the negotiator
jokes.punchline: An unidentified union worker quietly adds 'I don't' — immediately deflating Charlie's populist 'we know the truth' rally cry
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest one-liners. The structure is perfect: Charlie's increasingly confident populist speech ('we know the truth') punctured by one anonymous voice saying 'I don't.' Maximum economy — two words destroy the moment. The honest admission cuts through Charlie's performance. Great structural setup/payoff.

jokes.text: Look, just let me finish. This contract is bullshit. We gotta keep the strike going. Would you please just let him finish his sentence? But he's lying to us. But he hasn't said anything yet. Yeah, well, he's lying anyway.
jokes.setup: Charlie trying to foment worker unrest before the negotiator has spoken
jokes.punchline: 'But he hasn't said anything yet. Yeah, well, he's lying anyway.' — the circular logic of preemptive accusation; the lie is established in advance of any content
jokes.explanation: The 'he's lying anyway' preemptive accusation is a sharp satirical beat — capturing how populist rhetoric works by front-loading distrust before any facts are introduced. It's also a very Charlie move: reaching a confident conclusion before gathering any evidence. The dialogue's escalating absurdity is well-paced.

jokes.text: Hey, y'all, it's me, Martina Martinez. These white boys is crazy, right? Youse about to get screwed by your city and your union, as well.
jokes.setup: Dee arrives in disguise at the union meeting as 'Martina Martinez' to also foment unrest
jokes.punchline: Dee's ethnically coded persona — 'it's me, Martina Martinez' introduced as though everyone knows her — delivered in a broad accent, is cringeworthy and character-specifically terrible
jokes.explanation: Dee's Martina Martinez persona is classic Always Sunny cringe — not presented as funny but as an indictment of Dee's obliviousness. The 'Hey y'all, it's me' introduction implying a pre-existing relationship that doesn't exist is a good detail. The show's willingness to have characters do offensive things and frame the character, not the target, as the joke.

jokes.text: Okay, ma'am, if you just give me the mic, please... Rape! Rape! Rape! My... This white boy's got his hands all over my beautiful brown body!
jokes.setup: Negotiator tries to take the microphone back from Dee/Martina
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately screams 'Rape!' to the crowd, framing the microphone retrieval as sexual assault, then narrating it: 'This white boy's got his hands all over my beautiful brown body!' — weaponizing racial panic for a business dispute
jokes.explanation: Dark and uncomfortable — Dee deploying false accusation as an agitation tool, with the specific framing of racial grievance, is sharp satire about how inflammatory rhetoric works. 'My beautiful brown body' as Dee's self-narration is a great absurdist detail. The triple 'Rape! Rape! Rape!' is a good escalation. The horror is that it works on the crowd.

jokes.text: Now, why is it that my Latino and my proud African brothers got to be doing all the work while these cracker-ass bitches doing the negotiating?
jokes.setup: Dee/Martina in full demagogue mode at the union meeting
jokes.punchline: Dee performing intersectional solidarity she doesn't feel, using language she has no claim to ('cracker-ass bitches'), which is both offensive and somehow also an accurate political point — the show holding two contradictory things at once
jokes.explanation: The speech's content — white people doing the negotiating while minorities do the labor — is an accurate observation about labor dynamics, delivered by a white woman in brownface performing a fake identity. Always Sunny's satirical mode is to have terrible people accidentally make true points.

jokes.text: When was the last time a white lady pick up after you when you threw your orange soda and your grape sodas on the ground?!
jokes.setup: Dee/Martina escalating her racial grievance speech
jokes.punchline: Dee's rhetorical question incorporates a weirdly specific racist detail ('orange soda and your grape sodas') that reveals her actual stereotypical thinking beneath the solidarity performance — she's losing the crowd
jokes.explanation: The turn where Dee's performance cracks and her actual racist assumptions emerge — 'orange soda and your grape sodas' — is sharp writing. The specific plural 'grape sodas' is a great detail. The speech was always a performance; now we see the performer's real material. 'You're losing them' as the stage direction makes it even better.

jokes.text: What's happening over here?! The white upper-class man has no respect for us! They're dumping their trash in our neighborhood! ♪ So buy our classy gasoline ♪
jokes.setup: Dee trying to redirect the crowd after losing them; Charlie's gas song is audible outside
jokes.punchline: Dee pivots to the actual illegal dumping happening outside as evidence of white disrespect, then Charlie's gas jingle floats in — the gang's other plan accidentally providing Dee's rhetorical evidence
jokes.explanation: The convergence of plots — the illegal dumping providing Dee's real-time evidence, with Charlie's gas jingle audible as the soundtrack — is excellent plot construction. The gang's separate plans colliding creates escalating chaos. The ♪ classy gasoline ♪ snippet is perfectly timed absurdism.

jokes.text: Now, that looks to me like some sort of swarming mob. Yeah, I know. What are they so angry about though? I don't know. Something bad's about to happen to somebody. Is it us? Yep.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie watching an angry mob converge — a mob they caused
jokes.punchline: 'Something bad's about to happen to somebody. Is it us? Yep.' — the clinical analysis followed by the flat confirmation of their own victimhood
jokes.explanation: The 'Is it us? Yep.' exchange is brilliantly economical. The detached analytical framing of a mob they caused — 'some sort of swarming mob,' 'I don't know' — followed by the flat 'Yep' confirmation is very funny. The lack of urgency until the last possible second is characteristically Always Sunny. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Don't dump your trash in our neighborhood, you rich prick!
jokes.setup: The gang escaping from the mob they accidentally incited
jokes.punchline: The mob's grievance being completely legitimate — they DID dump trash there — makes the gang's victimhood richly ironic; they're being correctly punished
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff on the illegal dumping decision. The irony is correct but the line itself isn't particularly inspired — it's a good structural beat more than a great joke.

jokes.text: Don't dump your trash in our neighborhood, you rich prick! / Sorry! Sorry!
jokes.setup: The gang is fleeing the mob in their trash-covered limo
jokes.punchline: Being called 'rich pricks' while in a trash-covered limo, covered in seagulls, having just been chased by a mob — the gang's attempt at upper-class branding has completely failed
jokes.explanation: The irony of being called a rich prick while in a garbage-soaked limo is good structural payoff to the tuxedo plan, though it's not the sharpest execution.

jokes.text: What the hell were you guys doing dumping down there? Look, it would've been fine if Dee hadn't incited a race war.
jokes.setup: Frank confronting the others for creating the mob situation
jokes.punchline: Mac's explanation: it 'would've been fine' — the illegal dumping was not the problem — the problem was Dee 'inciting a race war' as a secondary consequence
jokes.explanation: 'It would've been fine if Dee hadn't incited a race war' is an excellent line — the casual use of 'incited a race war' as a slight operational hiccup, as though that's the only logistical flaw. Mac's framing normalizes the illegal environmental dumping and treats the race war as the administrative problem. Great economy and high quotability.

jokes.text: So what if he's gay, you know? He zigs, you zag. I would've gotten the contract.
jokes.setup: Post-mortem on the failed city official bribery plan
jokes.punchline: Frank reducing gay sexual identity to a chess move — 'He zigs, you zag' — as though Frank zigging (becoming sexually available to a man) was an obvious tactical option he regrets not taking
jokes.explanation: 'He zigs, you zag' as Frank's binary theory of gay encounter strategy is a great compressed Frank-ism. The implication that Frank considered becoming the sexual option is both darkly funny and totally in character. Good economy.

jokes.text: We should get rugs for the bar. We should make rugs for the bar. Make them? I got a rug guy. We could put on a show where we play rug salesmen.
jokes.setup: The gang decompressing after the trash plan failure, back at the bar
jokes.punchline: Within 30 seconds of returning to the bar, the gang is already planning a new scheme — and it escalates from 'get rugs' to 'put on a show where we play rug salesmen' in four steps
jokes.explanation: The speed at which a simple domestic need ('we should get rugs') becomes a theatrical performance concept ('put on a show where we play rug salesmen') is a perfect encapsulation of the gang's perpetual scheming. 'I got a rug guy' as a non-sequitur is a good Charlie beat.

jokes.text: Guys, we give up way too easily. Can we just not jump onto the next thing? What? That's insane.
jokes.setup: The gang immediately pivoting from the trash failure to a rug scheme
jokes.punchline: Frank — who proposed the trash plan that just catastrophically failed — accusing the gang of giving up too easily, while Dennis calls the idea of NOT giving up 'insane'
jokes.explanation: Frank's persistence with one more plan attempt while the gang's already moved to rugs is a good reversal — usually Frank has no investment in finishing. Dennis calling finishing what they started 'insane' is a good ironic beat.

jokes.text: Dennis, if you want to be classy and you're good with city councilmen and you think you can get him, great. Be classy and bang the guy. Go get him. I'll get him, but I'm not going to bang him. He's a twink versatile. You watch yourself. I wouldn't be able to satisfy him.
jokes.setup: Frank trying to revive the city official bribery plan
jokes.punchline: Dennis's principled objection isn't moral — it's capability-based: 'I wouldn't be able to satisfy him.' Mac warning 'You watch yourself' as though 'twink versatile' is a fighting word is excellent.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's concern being sexual competence rather than sexual willingness is a great character beat — he's not opposed to sleeping with the man, he's afraid he can't meet the standard. 'I wouldn't be able to satisfy him' as his final objection is both absurd and character-rich. Mac's 'You watch yourself' treating 'twink versatile' as a slur is a perfect reaction beat. High character integration.

jokes.text: Dennis, if you want to be classy and you're good with city councilmen and you think you can get him, great. Be classy and bang the guy.
jokes.setup: Frank tries to revive the original plan with adjustments
jokes.punchline: Frank's instruction to 'be classy' immediately followed by 'bang the guy' — the two concepts completely incompatible but delivered as if they go together naturally
jokes.explanation: 'Be classy and bang the guy' is a great Frank construction — the juxtaposition of 'classy' and 'bang the guy' in the same sentence of business advice is perfectly Frank. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Then we can strap me onto the back for the rest of the day. Everybody's happy.
jokes.setup: Mac presenting his contribution to the revised plan — taking over Dee's driving role and volunteering himself for the back
jokes.punchline: Mac enthusiastically volunteering to be strapped to the back of the vehicle 'for the rest of the day' as though this is an equal and desirable outcome for him
jokes.explanation: 'Everybody's happy' after Mac describes being strapped to the back of a vehicle is a good ironic button. Mac's acceptance of physical suffering as a reasonable role is both sad and funny.

jokes.text: Try the brakes. Try the... Did you cut the brakes again? Yep. Charlie. Why would you do that, Charlie? That's just what I do. Wild card, bitches!
jokes.setup: The gang has finally assembled their perfect revised plan; everyone is working together harmoniously
jokes.punchline: Charlie has cut the brakes. When asked why: 'That's just what I do. Wild card, bitches!' — vindicating everything the gang tried to suppress about him all episode
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of the series' most iconic beats. The structure is perfect: the entire episode has been building toward the gang suppressing the 'wild card' chaos, achieving a harmonious plan, reaching a moment of optimism — and Charlie immediately cuts the brakes, confirming everything. 'That's just what I do' is a beautiful five-word character statement. 'Wild card, bitches!' is the perfect cap. This earns 9+ on structure and character integration because it is the logical and inevitable conclusion of this character's entire arc, delivered with maximum commitment. Highly comparable to the calibration anchors — the structural payoff and quotability are exceptional.

jokes.text: Try the brakes. / Try the... Did you cut the brakes again? / Yep. / Charlie. / Why would you do that, Charlie? / That's just what I do. / Wild card, bitches! / What?
jokes.setup: The gang is driving their revised plan into action, congratulating themselves on working together better
jokes.punchline: Charlie has cut the brakes — his explanation 'That's just what I do' followed by 'Wild card, bitches!' is the payoff to the entire episode's wild card discussion
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of Always Sunny's great moments. The payoff to the wild card throughline is structurally perfect — the gang spent the entire episode trying to eliminate the wild card element, and Charlie has been patiently waiting to deploy it at maximum damage. 'That's just what I do' is devastating in its simplicity. 'Wild card, bitches!' has become a cultural catchphrase. The structure earns a 9 — 20 minutes of setup for a perfect 10-second payoff. Comparable to or exceeding the 9.5 anchor in terms of structural payoff, and the quotability is unquestionable.

jokes.text: Good call of getting those brakes fixed, Mac. Yeah, I saw that coming a mile away. All right, now that we got rid of our wild card, we can actually see this thing through.
jokes.setup: Charlie has apparently been ejected from the vehicle after cutting the brakes
jokes.punchline: Mac taking credit for 'seeing it coming' and Dennis reframing Charlie's self-sabotage as a fortuitous housecleaning — 'got rid of our wild card' — as though Charlie's brake-cutting was a gift
jokes.explanation: Mac's immediate revisionism — 'I saw that coming a mile away' — and Dennis's opportunistic silver lining are good character beats. The gang treating a vehicular crisis as a personnel management solution is very Always Sunny.

jokes.text: Guess the strike's over. Goddamn it. So, the rugs? Yeah, the rugs. Well, yeah, the rugs. Yeah, it's always been the rugs. Rugs are a great idea. Of course it's rugs. It's always been the rugs. We should get a billboard.
jokes.setup: The gang has just reassembled for the climactic trash plan execution
jokes.punchline: The strike ends literally the moment they're ready to execute — rendering everything pointless — and the gang immediately and unanimously pivots to rugs as though it was always the plan
jokes.explanation: The perfect structural ending. The strike resolving at the exact worst moment is classic sitcom anti-climax, but what elevates it is the gang's instant collective amnesia — 'it's always been the rugs' said with complete conviction by multiple people. The speed of the consensus and the uniform enthusiasm is the joke. 'We should get a billboard' as the final escalation into a new half-formed plan is a great button that sets up future recycled storylines. The episode's thesis — the gang perpetually recycles terrible plans — is delivered as the final joke. Structurally excellent.

tmdb_overview: With the garbage men of Philadelphia on strike, Frank concocts a plan to undercut the union and get the contract to collect the city's trash.
